people/papias/summary: Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the early second century who collected oral traditions from those who had known the apostles in his five-book Expositions of the Sayings of the Lord, now lost except for fragments quoted by Irenaeus and Eusebius. He is the earliest named witness to a literal, earthly thousand-year kingdom after the resurrection, and to traditions about the origins of Mark and Matthew.
people/papias/keyIdeas/0: Preferred the "living and abiding voice" of tradition to books
people/papias/keyIdeas/1: Expected a material millennial kingdom on earth
people/papias/keyIdeas/2: Early testimony about the Gospels of Mark and Matthew
people/tyconius/summary: North African Donatist lay theologian whose Book of Rules (c.382) was the first Latin handbook of biblical interpretation. His lost commentary on Revelation read the book as a description of the Church’s present struggle rather than a timetable of future events, and treated the thousand years as the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings. Though excommunicated by his own Donatist party for criticising its sectarianism, he deeply shaped Augustine and, through him, Western reading of the Apocalypse.
people/tyconius/keyIdeas/1: The Church is a mixed body (bipartite body of the Lord)
people/tyconius/keyIdeas/2: Revelation describes the Church’s present age, not a future timetable
people/c-h-dodd/summary: Welsh Congregationalist New Testament scholar at Manchester and Cambridge. In The Parables of the Kingdom (1935) he argued that Jesus proclaimed the kingdom of God as already present in his own ministry ("realized eschatology"), challenging Albert Schweitzer’s "consistent eschatology", which held that Jesus mistakenly expected an imminent end of the world. He later directed the translation of the New English Bible.
people/c-h-dodd/keyIdeas/1: The kerygma of the apostolic preaching
people/c-h-dodd/keyIdeas/2: Parables as crisis-announcements of the present kingdom
people/george-eldon-ladd/summary: American evangelical New Testament scholar at Fuller Seminary who popularised "inaugurated eschatology" (the kingdom as "already" present in Jesus but "not yet" consummated) among evangelicals, and defended historic (non-dispensational) premillennialism and a posttribulational return of Christ in The Blessed Hope (1956) and The Presence of the Future (1974).
people/john-of-leiden/roles/1: self-proclaimed king of the New Zion
people/john-of-leiden/summary: Dutch Melchiorite radical who, after the death of the prophet Jan Matthys in April 1534, ruled the besieged Westphalian city of Münster as "king" of a New Jerusalem, introducing community of goods and compulsory polygamy. After the city fell in June 1535 he was tortured and executed in January 1536; the iron cages that displayed the bodies still hang from the tower of St Lambert’s Church. Mainstream Anabaptists such as Menno Simons repudiated the episode.
people/john-of-leiden/keyIdeas/1: Armed resistance to hasten the end
people/manuel-lacunza/summary: Chilean Jesuit who, exiled to Imola in Italy after the suppression of the Jesuits in Spanish America (1767), wrote La venida del Mesías en gloria y majestad under the pen-name "Juan Josafat Ben-Ezra". Published in 1812 and placed on the Index in 1824, it argued for a future, literal millennial reign of Christ and a restoration of Israel. Edward Irving’s English translation (1827) fed directly into the British prophetic revival from which dispensationalism emerged, a notable Latin American contribution to modern premillennialism.
people/manuel-lacunza/keyIdeas/1: Future conversion and restoration of Israel
people/gelasius-i/summary: Bishop of Rome of North African descent whose letter Famuli vestrae pietatis (494) to Emperor Anastasius I distinguished the "sacred authority of the priests" from the "royal power" and claimed the greater weight for the former in spiritual matters. The "Gelasian dyarchy" became the charter text of medieval Western church–state theory.
people/gelasius-i/keyIdeas/1: Independence of the Church from imperial control
people/michael-sattler/summary: Former Benedictine prior of St Peter’s in the Black Forest who joined the Swiss Brethren and presided over the Schleitheim gathering (24 February 1527), whose "Brotherly Union" set out baptism of believers, the ban, separation from the world, nonresistance and refusal of oaths. He was tortured and burned at Rottenburg am Neckar in May 1527; his wife Margaretha was drowned.
people/michael-sattler/keyIdeas/0: Separation of the church from the world
people/michael-sattler/keyIdeas/1: Nonresistance: the sword is "outside the perfection of Christ"
people/frederick-douglass/summary: Born into slavery in Maryland, Douglass escaped in 1838 and became the most influential African American abolitionist. His Narrative (1845) and its appendix drew a sharp line between "the Christianity of Christ" and "the Christianity of this land" that defended slavery; he later advocated for women’s suffrage and civil rights.
people/frederick-douglass/keyIdeas/0: Slaveholding religion as a betrayal of Christ
people/thornton-stringfellow/summary: Virginia Baptist pastor and slaveholder whose A Brief Examination of Scripture Testimony on the Institution of Slavery (1841) became one of the most widely circulated biblical defences of American slavery. His arguments, from the patriarchs, the Mosaic law, Jesus’ silence and the apostolic household codes, are now universally rejected by the churches, including his own Southern Baptist tradition, which apologised for its defence of slavery in 1995.
people/thornton-stringfellow/keyIdeas/0: Slavery as sanctioned by God in both Testaments (historically argued, now repudiated)
people/martin-luther-king-jr/summary: African American Baptist minister who led the US civil rights movement from the Montgomery bus boycott (1955) to his assassination in Memphis (1968), combining Black church preaching, the Social Gospel, personalist theology and Gandhian nonviolence. His Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) defended civil disobedience against unjust laws, appealing to Augustine and Aquinas.
people/martin-luther-king-jr/keyIdeas/1: Unjust laws are no laws (after Augustine and Aquinas)
people/benjamin-b-warfield/summary: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield, the leading Old Princeton theologian, defended biblical inerrancy (with A. A. Hodge, 1881) and Calvinist orthodoxy. His Counterfeit Miracles (1918) gave cessationism its classic modern statement: the miraculous gifts authenticated the apostles and ceased with them. He held a postmillennial eschatology and, unusually for his circle, accepted that evolution could be compatible with Scripture.
people/john-romanides/summary: Greek-American Orthodox priest and professor at Thessaloniki whose doctoral thesis The Ancestral Sin (1957) argued that the Greek Fathers taught an inheritance of mortality and corruption from Adam, not of guilt, and sharply criticised Augustine’s influence on Western theology.
people/john-romanides/keyIdeas/0: Ancestral sin rather than inherited guilt
people/john-romanides/keyIdeas/1: Death as the power that drives sin
people/john-romanides/keyIdeas/2: Critique of Augustinian and scholastic theology
people/valerie-saiving/summary: American theologian whose 1960 essay “The Human Situation: A Feminine View” argued that defining sin chiefly as pride and self-assertion (Niebuhr, Nygren) reflects male experience; women’s typical temptation, she suggested, is rather self-negation and lack of a centred self. It is often regarded as a founding text of feminist theology.
people/valerie-saiving/keyIdeas/0: Gendered critique of sin as pride
people/nancey-murphy/summary: American philosopher at Fuller Theological Seminary, a member of the Church of the Brethren, who argues for “non-reductive physicalism”: humans are wholly physical beings whose higher capacities emerge from the brain, and Christian hope rests on bodily resurrection rather than an immortal soul.
people/matthias-flacius/summary: Lutheran theologian from Istria (Croatia), leader of the “Gnesio-Lutherans” and initiator of the Magdeburg Centuries. In a 1560 disputation with Viktorin Strigel he maintained that original sin is the very substance of fallen human nature, a view rejected in the Formula of Concord (1577).
people/matthias-flacius/keyIdeas/0: Original sin as substance of fallen humanity
people/helvidius/summary: Latin writer in Rome who argued (c. 380) that Mary had normal marital relations with Joseph after Jesus' birth and bore other children, and that virginity is not superior to marriage. Known only through Jerome's reply.
people/leo-iii-isaurian/summary: Byzantine emperor (717–741) who repelled the Arab siege of Constantinople (717–718) and is traditionally credited with beginning iconoclasm (c. 726–730). The extent of his iconoclast policy is debated by modern historians.
people/constantine-v/summary: Byzantine emperor (741–775), son of Leo III, the chief theologian of iconoclasm, who convened the Council of Hieria (754) and persecuted iconophile monks. A successful general, remembered hostilely in iconodule sources.
people/irene-of-athens/summary: Byzantine empress-regent and later sole ruler (797–802) who convened the Second Council of Nicaea (787) restoring icon veneration. Her rule as a woman was one pretext for Charlemagne's imperial coronation in 800.
people/theodore-the-studite/summary: Abbot of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, monastic reformer and leading defender of icons during the second iconoclasm, repeatedly exiled. His Antirrhetici argued that Christ's person is depicted in his circumscribable humanity.
people/theodore-the-studite/keyIdeas/2: Independence of the church from the emperor
people/henry-venn/roles/1: honorary secretary of the Church Missionary Society (1841–1872)
people/henry-venn/summary: Evangelical mission strategist who directed the Church Missionary Society for three decades and formulated the goal of "self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending" native churches, after which the foreign mission should withdraw ("the euthanasia of a mission"). He championed the consecration of Samuel Ajayi Crowther as the first African Anglican bishop (1864).
